Chaff clouds consist of numerous electrical dipoles of varying lengths to cover a broad radar frequency spectrum.
Dynamic RCS varies with target motion relative to radar, affecting frequency and aspect.
Turbulence increases the RCS of chaff clouds by 1.5 to 2.5 dBsm at 50 milliseconds.
Turbulence reduces the blooming time of chaff filaments by 25 to 50 milliseconds.
Turbulent kinetic energy (k) ranged from 17.5 to 18.375 m²/s² depending on ejection angle.
Reynolds number greater than 5×10^5 indicates turbulent boundary airflow relevant to chaff dispersion.
Chaff ejection velocity used in simulations was 35 m/s in the z-direction.
The standard k-epsilon turbulence model was used for CFD simulations.
1000 chaff filaments of four different lengths were modeled for RCS analysis.
ANSYS Fluent simulations were performed in transient mode with time steps to capture blooming dynamics.
ANSYS HFSS-IE used finite element method with triangular meshing of chaff surfaces for RCS calculation.
Turbulence has a greater effect on chaff ejected perpendicularly (90°) than parallel (0°) to aircraft movement.
The RCS of non-turbulent chaff at 100 ms matches turbulent chaff at 50 ms, showing turbulence accelerates blooming.
Chaff blooming phases include transient, bloom, mature, and decay stages.
The study used fluid properties at 4000 m altitude for realistic simulation conditions.
Pressure boundary conditions were applied at inlet and outlet in CFD model.
Particles were tracked using stochastic discrete random walk and eddy lifetime models.
Chaff filament RCS is averaged over random orientations assuming isotropic distribution.
Turbulence enhances inter-dipole spacing, increasing RCS during initial chaff firing.
The study extrapolates results to practical scenarios with millions of chaff filaments.
